options.a: Lights, mirrors, emergency exits, tires, brakes, and required safety equipment
options.b: Engine fluids and tires, with lights and mirrors checked on arrival at the school
options.c: Brakes and tires, leaving emergency exits for the monthly drill
options.d: Lights and mirrors, with brakes left to the mechanic's weekly test

distractorExplanations.b: Lights and mirrors are checked before leaving the lot; a bus cannot begin a route with misadjusted mirrors or dead warning lights.
distractorExplanations.c: Emergency exits are part of every pre-trip; evacuation drills are separate from confirming the exits open and their alarms work.
distractorExplanations.d: Brake checks are part of the driver's pre-trip every day; a weekly mechanic check does not replace them.

options.a: Show the area directly in front of the bumper, which crossover mirrors cannot
options.b: Show wide areas along the sides and front danger zones that flat mirrors may miss
options.c: Show the true distance and size of vehicles beside the bus for lane changes
options.d: Show the area behind the bus so backing is safe without a lookout

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses convex with crossover mirrors; crossover mirrors cover the area in front of the bumper, while convex mirrors cover the sides.
distractorExplanations.c: Convex mirrors make objects appear smaller and farther away than they really are, so they do not show true distance.
distractorExplanations.d: Convex mirrors do not show directly behind the bus; backing still needs a responsible lookout and extreme caution.

options.a: The area within 3 feet of the bus where students touch the body or wheels
options.b: The 50-foot stopping zone in front of the bus where traffic must halt
options.c: The area extending about 10 feet around the bus where students are at greatest risk
options.d: The road ahead between where the amber lights start and where the red lights activate

distractorExplanations.a: Too narrow: the danger zone extends about 10 feet from the sides and rear and up to 30 feet from the front bumper.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the danger zone with traffic stopping distances; the danger zone is the area around the bus where students are struck.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the 8-light warning sequence distance with the danger zone that surrounds the stopped bus.

options.a: Keep driving and check the exit at the next scheduled student stop
options.b: Ask the nearest student to close it while the bus keeps moving
options.c: Report it on the post-trip form, since exit buzzers often false-alarm
options.d: Stop safely and secure/close the exit properly before continuing

distractorExplanations.a: An open exit while moving is an immediate hazard; stop safely now rather than waiting for the next stop.
distractorExplanations.b: A student moving to an open exit while the bus is underway risks a fall; the driver stops first and secures it.
distractorExplanations.c: Treating the buzzer as a false alarm ignores a possibly open exit; stop and verify before continuing.

options.a: Stop other traffic while students board or leave the bus as required by law
options.b: Warn traffic that the bus is preparing to stop within the next 100 to 300 feet
options.c: Signal that the bus is about to stop at a railroad crossing just ahead
options.d: Show other drivers they may pass slowly on the left while students load

distractorExplanations.b: That is the job of the amber lights; red lights and the stop arm mean the bus has stopped and traffic must stop.
distractorExplanations.c: Railroad stops use hazard warning lamps, not the red lights or stop arm, which are reserved for student loading.
distractorExplanations.d: Red lights and an extended stop arm require traffic to stop, not to pass slowly.

options.a: Inflation judged by eye, plus tread of at least 2/32 inch on the front tires
options.b: Proper inflation, tread, and no dangerous cuts/bulges or duals touching
options.c: Tread depth only, since inflation is checked by the fuel-island crew
options.d: Inflation and tread, with recapped tires allowed on the front wheels

distractorExplanations.a: Pressure needs a gauge, and front steering tires need at least 4/32-inch tread, not 2/32.
distractorExplanations.c: Inflation is part of the driver's pre-trip check; low pressure causes blowouts and handling problems.
distractorExplanations.d: Recapped or retreaded tires are not allowed on the front wheels of a bus; that allowance applies to rear wheels.

options.a: The service brakes have failed and the bus must not move at all
options.b: ABS is off, so pump the brakes rapidly in every stop until it is repaired
options.c: ABS may not function; drive carefully and get repairs—use normal braking
options.d: The lamp stayed on after startup, so shutting down and restarting clears the fault

distractorExplanations.a: An ABS lamp signals an ABS fault; the foundation service brakes still work, so you drive carefully and get repairs.
distractorExplanations.b: Rapid pumping is not standard braking; without ABS you brake normally and carefully to avoid wheel lockup.
distractorExplanations.d: A lamp that stays on after the startup bulb check indicates a fault; restarting the engine does not repair ABS.

cdl-school-bus-readiness-check-vehicle-e.explanation: ABS faults do not eliminate foundation brakes; drive carefully, get repairs, and use normal braking without pumping in panic stops.

options.a: Kept in the transportation office and issued for field trips
options.b: Present, with body fluid kits needed on special-needs buses alone
options.c: Present and sealed, with contents checked during the annual inspection
options.d: Present, accessible, and stocked per state/district requirements

distractorExplanations.a: Required kits ride on the bus on every route, not just on field trips.
distractorExplanations.b: Body fluid cleanup kits are needed on regular routes too; illness and injuries happen on any bus.
distractorExplanations.c: A kit used during a route is restocked promptly; waiting for the annual inspection leaves it empty.

options.a: Charged, properly mounted, and accessible to the driver
options.b: Charged and stored in a rear compartment away from students
options.c: Present, with the gauge checked only during annual inspection
options.d: Mounted near the rear emergency door for student use in a fire

distractorExplanations.b: A rear compartment is not readily accessible to the driver; it is mounted where it can be grabbed quickly.
distractorExplanations.c: The gauge and seal are checked on every pre-trip; a discharged unit could otherwise go unnoticed for months.
distractorExplanations.d: Extinguishers are mounted for the driver's access; students evacuate rather than fight fires.

options.a: Slow to 20 mph with flashers on and continue to the next stop
options.b: Stop in a safe place and not continue until visibility is safe
options.c: Turn on the defroster and continue, since it clears the glass
options.d: Finish the route, then report the wipers on the post-trip form

distractorExplanations.a: Without wipers, visibility in heavy rain is inadequate at any speed; stop safely rather than continue.
distractorExplanations.c: Defrosters clear fog on the inside, not heavy rain on the outside; working wipers are required.
distractorExplanations.d: Failed wipers in heavy rain are an immediate safety defect; reporting them later does not make continuing safe.

cdl-school-bus-readiness-check-vehicle-e.explanation: Inadequate visibility is a stop condition; student involvement outside a moving bus is dangerous. Continue only once repairs are made per policy.

options.a: Required only on highway segments, with release allowed at student stops
options.b: Optional, since the compartmentalized seat design protects the driver
options.c: Required/expected—drivers must use the driver restraint as designed
options.d: Required on buses over 10,000 pounds, optional on Type A small buses

distractorExplanations.a: The driver stays belted whenever the bus is moving; belt use is not tied to highway segments.
distractorExplanations.b: Compartmentalization protects passengers in their seats; the driver's seat is not compartmentalized, so the belt is needed.
distractorExplanations.d: Driver restraints are required on every school bus type; small Type A buses are not exempt.

options.a: Kept locked during routes to prevent students opening them
options.b: Checked during the semi-annual evacuation drill, not each pre-trip
options.c: Inspected by maintenance, since drivers check only side exits
options.d: Operational, unobstructed, and included in pre-trip checks

distractorExplanations.a: Locked hatches defeat egress in a rollover; they must open from inside without a key.
distractorExplanations.b: Drills are separate from daily inspection; hatch operation and warning devices are checked on pre-trips.
distractorExplanations.c: Drivers check every emergency exit, roof hatches included, on each pre-trip inspection.

options.a: Safety, security, and operational accountability per district policy
options.b: Letting dispatch supervise riders so the driver can focus on the road
options.c: Replacing the driver's student count at each stop with GPS rider logs
options.d: Giving parents live video access to the bus during routes

distractorExplanations.b: Cameras record but do not supervise in real time; the driver stays responsible for students aboard.
distractorExplanations.c: GPS logs do not verify that each student is clear of the danger zone; the driver still counts.
distractorExplanations.d: Live parent or public video access raises privacy issues and is not the purpose; footage is accessed per district policy.

options.a: Tighter adjustment lets the slack adjusters hold the parking brake
options.b: Out-of-adjustment brakes trigger the low-air warning at 60 psi
options.c: Excessive pushrod travel reduces braking effectiveness
options.d: Self-adjusting slack adjusters mean adjustment needs no driver check

distractorExplanations.a: Spring brakes hold the parked bus; adjustment matters because excess pushrod travel weakens all braking.
distractorExplanations.b: The low-air warning reflects reservoir pressure, not brake adjustment; poor adjustment shows up as excess pushrod travel.
distractorExplanations.d: Automatic slack adjusters can fail or mask a problem; drivers still check pushrod stroke during inspection.

options.a: They walk 3 feet in front of the bumper and wave to the driver
options.b: The driver signals it is safe and they have checked traffic themselves
options.c: The red lights come on, which means all traffic has stopped
options.d: The bus door closes, which tells them the driver is ready for them to go across

distractorExplanations.a: Students walk about 10 feet ahead of the bus to where they can see the driver, not 3 feet where they are hidden.
distractorExplanations.c: Red lights do not guarantee traffic has stopped; students wait for the driver's signal and look for themselves.
distractorExplanations.d: A closing door does not mean it is safe to cross; students wait for the driver's crossing signal.

options.a: Pick up the papers quickly before the driver closes the door
options.b: Signal the driver with a wave, then retrieve them right away
options.c: Tell the driver and wait for instructions—never go under/near wheels
options.d: Wait until the bus starts to pull away, then go back quickly for the papers

distractorExplanations.a: Bending down near the bus is exactly when students vanish from the driver's view; they tell the driver first.
distractorExplanations.b: A wave does not confirm the driver saw it; students wait for the driver's instructions before going near the bus.
distractorExplanations.d: Returning toward a moving bus puts the student in the danger zone; the driver must know and give instructions.

options.a: Stopping within 10 feet of the nearest rail, then crossing
options.b: Slowing and looking, with a full stop when signals flash
options.c: Stopping, then shifting gears on the tracks if the bus slows
options.d: Stopping, looking and listening, and crossing only when safe

distractorExplanations.a: The stop is made 15 to 50 feet from the nearest rail; closer than 15 feet risks the bus being struck.
distractorExplanations.b: School buses stop at crossings even without active signals unless an exempt sign or rule applies.
distractorExplanations.c: Gears are not shifted while crossing; the gear is selected before starting across.

cdl-school-bus-readiness-check-loading-u.explanation: School buses must follow railroad stop requirements, with required hazards and procedures; never stop on the tracks.

options.a: Evacuate students immediately away from the tracks at an angle toward the train's approach
options.b: Evacuate students away from the tracks in the same direction the train is traveling
options.c: Keep students seated while you radio dispatch to have the train stopped first
options.d: Try to restart the bus and clear the tracks before ordering an evacuation

distractorExplanations.b: Moving in the train's direction of travel puts students in the debris path; they go at an angle toward the approaching train.
distractorExplanations.c: Radio calls waste critical seconds; evacuate first, then notify the railroad and dispatch.
distractorExplanations.d: With a train coming, evacuation comes first; restart attempts can cost the time needed to get students clear.

options.a: Directly behind the bus, where traffic cannot reach them
options.b: To a safe location away from traffic as directed
options.c: Along the side of the bus toward the rear wheels
options.d: Across the road at once, before traffic starts moving

distractorExplanations.a: Behind the bus is a driver blind spot and a backing hazard; students move ahead and away from traffic.
distractorExplanations.c: The area along the side near the rear wheels is a danger zone; students move away from the bus.
distractorExplanations.d: Crossing happens on the driver's signal after traffic stops; hurrying across risks being struck.

cdl-school-bus-readiness-check-loading-u.explanation: Safe waiting/walking paths keep students out of traffic and wheel areas, remaining visible to the driver as required.

options.a: The rider count matches the district roster for reimbursement
options.b: Students are seated before the bus reaches the next stop
options.c: All students are accounted for and none are left around the danger zone unseen
options.d: The driver can skip the right-side mirror check once the count matches the list

distractorExplanations.a: Roster counts serve administration, but the safety reason is confirming no one is left in the danger zone.
distractorExplanations.b: Seating is a separate check; the loading count confirms every student boarded or cleared the danger zone.
distractorExplanations.d: A matching count supplements mirror checks; it does not replace looking for students near the bus.

options.a: The bus is preparing to stop to load/unload students
options.b: The bus has stopped and traffic must now stop in both directions
options.c: The bus is stopping at a railroad crossing ahead
options.d: Students have finished boarding and the bus is pulling out

distractorExplanations.b: That describes the red lights and stop arm; ambers warn that the bus is about to stop.
distractorExplanations.c: Railroad stops use hazard warning lamps, not the amber student-stop lights.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the sequence: ambers come on before the stop, not after loading as the bus departs.

options.a: Signal students to cross once the violating car has passed the bus
options.b: Keep students from crossing until traffic is safe; report violators per policy
options.c: Wave students across while honking the horn to warn the next car approaching fast
options.d: Unload students on the far side so they can cross behind the bus

distractorExplanations.a: Another vehicle may follow the violator; students wait until every lane of traffic is stopped and safe.
distractorExplanations.c: A horn does not stop traffic; students stay put until traffic is stopped.
distractorExplanations.d: Crossing behind the bus is a classic fatality pattern; students cross in front, on signal, when traffic is stopped.

options.a: Allowed on school grounds if a student lookout signals the driver from the rear
options.b: Avoided on routes but routine at stops, using the backup alarm instead of a lookout
options.c: Avoided when possible; if required, use a responsible adult lookout and extreme caution
options.d: Done after students have unloaded at the stop so they are not aboard during backing

distractorExplanations.a: Students are not used as backing lookouts; a responsible adult is needed, with students aboard or well clear.
distractorExplanations.b: Backing at student stops is discouraged or prohibited, and a backup alarm does not replace a lookout.
distractorExplanations.d: Backing after unloading puts students on the ground behind the bus; load them first, or do not back at all.

options.a: Cross once the near lanes stop, since far-lane drivers can see the bus's red lights
options.b: Cross at the nearest corner crosswalk rather than in front of the bus
options.c: Cross close in front of the bumper so the stop arm shields them
options.d: Cross only after traffic has stopped and the driver gives the crossing signal

distractorExplanations.a: Students cross when every lane has stopped; far-lane traffic on a multi-lane road may not stop.
distractorExplanations.b: Leaving the bus to use a corner crosswalk takes students out of the driver's view and protection.
distractorExplanations.c: Close to the bumper students are hidden; they walk about 10 feet ahead where the driver can see them.

cdl-school-bus-readiness-check-loading-u.explanation: Front crossing in view is the standard; students walk far enough in front to stay in view. Rear/out-of-sight crossing is forbidden.

options.a: Open the door/window as required to look and listen for trains
options.b: Keep the door closed and turn off the radio and fans to listen
options.c: Look both ways once, then cross if the signals are not flashing
options.d: Have a student by the door watch for trains while you check mirrors

distractorExplanations.b: Turning off noise sources helps, but the forward door and driver window are opened so the driver can hear trains.
distractorExplanations.c: Signals can fail; the driver looks and listens in both directions, more than once, before crossing.
distractorExplanations.d: The driver cannot delegate the look-and-listen to students; it is the driver's own responsibility.

options.a: Safer than same-side loading because students face the bus while crossing
options.b: Especially hazardous—use proper signals and ensure all traffic is stopped
options.c: Allowed with amber lights alone, since red lights confuse oncoming traffic
options.d: Handled by having students cross before the bus arrives at the stop

distractorExplanations.a: Crossing exposes students to traffic in the roadway; same-side loading avoids that conflict entirely.
distractorExplanations.c: Reds and the stop arm stop traffic for crossing students; ambers just warn that a stop is coming.
distractorExplanations.d: Students wait on their side until the bus stops and the driver signals; crossing early is unprotected.

cdl-school-bus-readiness-check-loading-u.explanation: Crossing students face more traffic conflict; ensure all traffic is stopped before students enter the roadway.

options.a: Wait for the school staff signal, which confirms the whole danger zone is clear
options.b: Count students who exited and pull away when the number matches
options.c: Check mirrors and the danger zone carefully for late students and pedestrians
options.d: Sound the horn twice and pull away slowly so students can step back

distractorExplanations.a: Staff help, but the driver still checks mirrors and the danger zone personally before moving.
distractorExplanations.b: A matching count does not detect late runners or pedestrians near the bus; mirror checks are still needed.
distractorExplanations.d: Horns do not replace looking; students may not hear or react in time.

options.a: Protect students—stop safely, assess, and follow emergency procedures
options.b: Call dispatch first and wait for instructions before deciding to stop
options.c: Protect the bus and equipment so the district can recover costs later
options.d: Evacuate the bus at once in every emergency before assessing hazards

distractorExplanations.b: Students come first; stop safely and assess, then contact dispatch rather than delaying for instructions.
distractorExplanations.c: Property is secondary; the life safety of students is the first responsibility.
distractorExplanations.d: Evacuation is not always safest; the driver assesses first, since leaving the bus can expose students to traffic.

cdl-school-bus-readiness-check-student-m.explanation: Life safety and orderly emergency action come before property or debate, including evacuation procedures as needed.

options.a: Keep driving to school and let the principal deal with them there
options.b: Stop the bus safely when needed, separate them using district-approved methods
options.c: Stop the bus in the nearest travel lane and restrain both students by physical force
options.d: Separate them by verbal commands while driving, without stopping

distractorExplanations.a: A fight while moving distracts the driver and injures students; stop safely and intervene now.
distractorExplanations.c: Stopping in a lane creates a crash hazard, and force beyond district methods escalates risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Managing a fight while driving divides attention; stop safely when needed, then separate them.

cdl-school-bus-readiness-check-student-m.explanation: Safe stop and controlled intervention protect everyone; document the fight and report the incident afterward.

options.a: Take backpacks and belongings so nothing is left in a burning bus
options.b: Exit through the front door only, oldest students first
options.c: Leave quickly in an orderly way using designated exits without pushing
options.d: Stay seated until the driver confirms there is a fire, then run to the nearest exits

distractorExplanations.a: Belongings slow evacuation in fire or smoke; students leave them behind.
distractorExplanations.b: Drills teach use of rear and side exits too, and evacuation order goes by seat position, not age.
distractorExplanations.d: Drills teach an orderly exit without running or pushing; waiting and then rushing causes injuries.

options.a: Drive the student to the nearest hospital yourself, skipping the remaining stops
options.b: Give the student their own prescribed medication from their backpack
options.c: Continue to school, where the nurse can provide care within minutes
options.d: Secure the bus, request emergency help per policy, and provide appropriate first aid

distractorExplanations.a: Transporting an ill student is generally against policy; stop, secure the bus and call EMS rather than driving them.
distractorExplanations.b: Administering medication requires authorization; drivers follow the student's plan and call for help.
distractorExplanations.c: Delaying care in a medical emergency is unsafe; secure the bus and request help immediately.

cdl-school-bus-readiness-check-student-m.explanation: Stop, communicate, and aid within training/policy; first aid stays within the driver's training and privacy still matters.

options.a: Following district emergency protocols—do not attempt heroics
options.b: Confiscating the weapon yourself before notifying anyone else
options.c: Searching every student's backpack before the next stop
options.d: Waiting until arrival at school to tell the principal

distractorExplanations.b: Confronting a student for a weapon can escalate violence; follow protocol and involve law enforcement.
distractorExplanations.c: Mass searches by the driver are not the protocol; secure safety and notify authorities per policy.
distractorExplanations.d: Weapons need immediate notification per protocol, not a report at the end of the route.

cdl-school-bus-readiness-check-student-m.explanation: Trained protocol, communication, and law enforcement involvement take priority; heroics escalate danger.

options.a: Strict discipline through loud warnings on the first day of school
options.b: Clear rules, consistent enforcement, and respectful communication
options.c: Letting students choose seats freely so they are content on the ride
options.d: Referring every minor issue directly to the principal for discipline

distractorExplanations.a: Loud warnings set a fear-based tone; consistent, respectful enforcement prevents problems more reliably.
distractorExplanations.c: Assigned seating is a key management tool; free seating often increases conflict and reduces supervision.
distractorExplanations.d: Drivers handle minor issues on the bus with progressive discipline; referral is for serious or repeated problems.

options.a: Pull over immediately and put the student off the bus at the roadside to walk
options.b: Brake firmly so the student learns to stay seated when the bus moves
options.c: Address it using approved progressive discipline; stop if safety requires
options.d: Ignore it until the student's stop, then report it to the parents

distractorExplanations.a: Students are not put off the bus anywhere except their own stop or school; doing so endangers the child.
distractorExplanations.b: Using vehicle motion as punishment is abusive and can injure every rider.
distractorExplanations.d: A hazard on board needs action now under progressive discipline; waiting until the stop leaves the hazard.

options.a: Parking under a highway overpass with students kept seated until the storm passes
options.b: Staying on the bus with windows open to equalize pressure during the storm
options.c: Evacuating to the bus's lee side and having students stand close against it
options.d: Seeking appropriate shelter per emergency plans rather than staying exposed on the road

distractorExplanations.a: Overpasses funnel wind and debris and are dangerous tornado shelters; follow the plan to a sturdy building or low ditch.
distractorExplanations.b: Opening windows to equalize pressure is a myth; it wastes time and adds glass and debris risk.
distractorExplanations.c: A bus can be rolled by tornado winds; students go to a sturdy building or low ditch away from the bus.

options.a: Fire, fuel leak, or stalling in a dangerous location make staying aboard unsafe
options.b: Any collision occurs, since students must leave a damaged bus immediately
options.c: The bus breaks down anywhere, even on a quiet road with no hazard
options.d: Heavy traffic surrounds the bus, so students wait on the shoulder

distractorExplanations.b: Many minor collisions are safer handled with students aboard; evacuate when staying is the greater danger.
distractorExplanations.c: A breakdown in a safe location usually means staying aboard; leaving puts students near traffic needlessly.
distractorExplanations.d: Heavy traffic outside is a reason to stay aboard; the shoulder exposes students to passing vehicles.

options.a: Speed up unloading, since younger students exit at earlier stops
options.b: Improve supervision and reduce unsafe behavior in harder-to-see areas
options.c: Keep younger students away from the rear exit in case of a crash
options.d: Free the rear seats for older students to supervise younger ones

distractorExplanations.a: Seating young riders up front is about supervision, not the order of stops.
distractorExplanations.c: Every seat is compartmentalized; the purpose of front seating is closer supervision, not crash position.
distractorExplanations.d: Older students are not supervisors; the driver keeps young riders close for visibility and control.

options.a: Wait for a parent complaint before taking any action on the bus
options.b: Move the targeted student to a new seat and keep it confidential
options.c: Intervene appropriately, document, and report per school policy
options.d: Confront the bully in front of the other riders to set an example

distractorExplanations.a: Drivers act on suspected bullying without waiting for complaints; it is part of the school's safety climate.
distractorExplanations.b: Moving the victim alone does not address the behavior; the incident must be documented and reported.
distractorExplanations.d: Public confrontation can escalate; intervene appropriately and follow reporting procedures.

options.a: Letting the parent board to discuss the issue privately at the back of the bus
options.b: Closing the door and driving off immediately to end the confrontation
options.c: Resolving the dispute on the spot yourself so the route does not run late for students
options.d: Student safety, calm communication, and involving school administrators/law enforcement

distractorExplanations.a: Unauthorized adults do not board; it can put students at risk. Keep the parent off and call for support.
distractorExplanations.b: Driving off with someone at the door is dangerous; secure students, stay calm and call for help.
distractorExplanations.c: Schedule is not the priority; involve administrators or police rather than handling a hostile adult alone.

options.a: Current and available so you can communicate during incidents
options.b: Kept at the dispatch office, with drivers calling in for details
options.c: Updated at the start of each school year and not revised after
options.d: Posted on the bus window so substitutes can read them easily

distractorExplanations.b: Radios fail and dispatch may be unavailable; route and contact sheets must be on the bus.
distractorExplanations.c: Student contacts and routes change mid-year; sheets must be kept current.
distractorExplanations.d: Posting student information publicly breaches privacy; keep it accessible to the driver but not displayed.

options.a: Stop, evacuate, and move students downwind so the smoke blows away from them
options.b: Stop in a safe place, evacuate, and move students upwind to a safe distance
options.c: Keep students aboard while you open the hood to find the source
options.d: Drive to the nearest fire station, keeping students seated

distractorExplanations.a: Downwind is where the smoke travels; students move upwind, at least 100 feet from the bus.
distractorExplanations.c: Opening the hood feeds oxygen to a fire; evacuate students before investigating.
distractorExplanations.d: Continuing with smoke risks a fire with students aboard; stop safely and evacuate now.

cdl-school-bus-readiness-check-student-m.explanation: Smoke/fire risk demands evacuation away from the vehicle and traffic hazards; shut down as appropriate and move students upwind.

options.a: Shared with substitute drivers by posting it on the dashboard
options.b: Discussed with the student's classmates so they can help
options.c: Used only as needed for safe transport and kept private
options.d: Kept at home by the driver for reference on weekends

distractorExplanations.a: Substitutes may need the information, but posting it openly exposes it to riders and the public.
distractorExplanations.b: Classmates have no need to know; confidential plans are shared with those who need them for transport.
distractorExplanations.d: Confidential records stay under district control; they are kept secure and used for transport purposes.

options.a: Operating with students aboard while using a hand-held phone for non-emergency chatting
options.b: Using a hands-free two-way radio to tell dispatch about a road hazard on the route
options.c: Turning on the eight-light warning system before stopping at a student pickup point
options.d: Opening the front door and driver's window to listen for trains at railroad crossings

distractorExplanations.b: Brief hands-free radio contact with dispatch is a normal, permitted part of operations, not the prohibited act.
distractorExplanations.c: Activating the ambers before a stop is required procedure, not a prohibited action.
distractorExplanations.d: Opening the door and window at railroad crossings is required procedure in many states, not prohibited.

options.a: Limited to a 0.08 blood alcohol level, the same as for car drivers
options.b: Strictly prohibited—school bus drivers are held to high safety standards
options.c: Allowed for prescription opioids if taken more than an hour before driving
options.d: Prohibited on student routes, but allowed before deadhead or charter runs

distractorExplanations.a: CDL holders face a 0.04 limit in a CMV and are out of service at any detectable level; 0.08 is the car standard.
distractorExplanations.c: Drugs that impair driving are prohibited even with a prescription; timing does not make impairment safe.
distractorExplanations.d: Alcohol and drug rules apply to all safety-sensitive driving, including deadhead and charter trips.

options.a: Allowed for under 5 minutes if the engine is off and the keys are removed
options.b: Allowed if an older student is placed in charge of the bus
options.c: Prohibited—drivers must supervise or follow approved handoff procedures
options.d: Allowed at school if the bus is parked in the loading zone

distractorExplanations.a: There is no short-stop allowance; students may not be left unattended for any period.
distractorExplanations.b: Students cannot be designated supervisors; an authorized adult handoff is required.
distractorExplanations.d: Even at school, students are not left alone on the bus without an approved handoff.

options.a: Allowed up to 5 mph over the posted school-zone limit
options.b: Permitted with hazard lights on to warn other drivers
options.c: Acceptable if dispatch approves to keep the schedule
options.d: Illegal and unsafe—lateness never justifies speeding

distractorExplanations.a: There is no 5 mph tolerance; posted school-zone limits apply to buses exactly as written.
distractorExplanations.b: Hazard lights do not authorize speeding; they are for stopped or slow-moving situations.
distractorExplanations.c: Dispatch cannot authorize breaking speed laws; schedule pressure does not override them.

options.a: Are limited; know state rules—do not assume you may blow crossings
options.b: Apply at every crossing marked by a white X-shaped crossbuck sign
options.c: Apply whenever the crossing has active flashing lights and gates
options.d: Apply to crossings within 500 feet of a school, where trains run slowly

distractorExplanations.b: Crossbucks mark public crossings in general; exemptions apply where a posted EXEMPT sign or state rule allows.
distractorExplanations.c: Active signals do not create an exemption; buses still stop at signaled crossings unless an exempt rule applies.
distractorExplanations.d: Proximity to a school is not an exemption; stop requirements follow the posted signs and state rule.

options.a: Acceptable if the bus was fully inspected by another driver the previous afternoon
options.b: A serious violation that can lead to termination and legal consequences
options.c: A minor paperwork issue if the defects found were small
options.d: Permitted when the supervisor signs off on the report as well

distractorExplanations.a: Yesterday's inspection does not make today's report true; signing for a check you did not do is falsification.
distractorExplanations.c: Falsification is a serious violation whatever the defect size; the record must reflect what was inspected.
distractorExplanations.d: A supervisor's signature does not legitimize a false report; both may face consequences.

options.a: Allowed for parents riding to check on their own children
options.b: Allowed for district employees showing their staff ID
options.c: Against policy/rules unless specifically authorized
options.d: Allowed for adults if a seat is empty and they sit up front

distractorExplanations.a: Parents still need district authorization to ride; being a parent is not an exception.
distractorExplanations.b: Staff ID alone is not authorization to ride a student route; riders must be specifically authorized.
distractorExplanations.d: An empty seat does not authorize an unassigned adult; it creates supervision and liability risk.

options.a: Allowed on short routes when every seat is filled three to a seat
options.b: Permitted behind the standee line, as on transit buses
options.c: Allowed for older students who hold the seat backs firmly
options.d: Prohibited—students must be properly seated as required

distractorExplanations.a: There is no short-route exception; overflow requires another bus, not standees.
distractorExplanations.b: The standee line applies to transit buses; school bus students are seated while the bus moves.
distractorExplanations.c: Holding a seat back is not restraint; sudden stops throw standing students.

options.a: Illegal for other motorists and extremely dangerous to students
options.b: Legal on a divided highway for traffic following behind the bus
options.c: Legal for drivers passing on the right shoulder at low speed
options.d: A civil violation only, since it is captured by stop-arm cameras

distractorExplanations.b: Traffic behind the bus must stop even on divided highways; opposing traffic across a median may be the exempt group.
distractorExplanations.c: Passing on the right is where students exit; it is illegal and among the deadliest violations.
distractorExplanations.d: Camera enforcement does not reduce the offense; it remains a traffic violation and a danger to students.

options.a: Fatigue mainly affects night drivers, not those on morning routes
options.b: Fatigue impairs reaction time and increases crash risk with children aboard
options.c: Coffee and an open window offset fatigue for a short route
options.d: Hours limits are mainly about payroll records for split-shift school bus drivers

distractorExplanations.a: Early-morning routes after short sleep are a fatigue risk; impairment depends on rest, not time of day.
distractorExplanations.c: Stimulants and fresh air do not restore alertness; adequate rest does.
distractorExplanations.d: Hours rules exist to prevent fatigued driving, not to manage payroll.

options.a: Allowed for quick stops if the students stay seated with the doors shut
options.b: Allowed for fuel or food stops that take less than ten minutes
options.c: Prohibited—routes and vehicle use must follow authorized purposes
options.d: Permitted if dispatch is told about the stop by radio beforehand

distractorExplanations.a: A seated, closed-door bus is still being misused; unauthorized stops violate policy and delay students.
distractorExplanations.b: Duration does not make a personal errand authorized; route deviations require approval.
distractorExplanations.d: Notifying dispatch is not authorization; personal errands with students aboard are prohibited.

options.a: Minimize unnecessary idling for health/environmental and policy compliance
options.b: Idle at least 15 minutes before routes to warm the engine in all seasons
options.c: Keep engines running in school loading zones so heat and AC stay on
options.d: Shut off the engine at railroad crossings to reduce exhaust near tracks

distractorExplanations.b: Modern diesels need just a few minutes of warm-up; long idling wastes fuel and exposes students to exhaust.
distractorExplanations.c: Many districts and states specifically limit idling in loading zones because students breathe the exhaust.
distractorExplanations.d: Shutting off at a crossing risks a stall on the tracks; idling limits apply to waiting areas, not crossings.
